idiom_name: routing loop over an ordered (selector -> queue id) dispatch table; System V msgrcv type selection for brokerless queues
implementation_notes: C has no router runtime, so the classic structure is written by hand: a router loop reads from the input queue or socket, the message header carries a route selector, and an ordered array of {selector, destination} rules selects the outbound queue the untouched buffer is written to. System V queues give type-directed selection for free - msgrcv(msqid, &buf, sz, msgtyp, 0) returns only messages whose mtype equals msgtyp - so a consumer-side router can select by type without any dispatch table, but that only works while the decision maps one-to-one onto the mtype field and the consumer, not the router, chooses the type. The hand-written routing loop remains justified whenever one message must be chosen among several destinations, when rules come from a configuration file, or when a message must be republished (a msgrcv-based split leaves the message on the queue it was read from unless you forward it explicitly).
pitfalls: The msgbuf layout is caller-defined but fixed at compile time: messages longer than msgsz fail with E2BIG and, without MSG_NOERROR, are never removed from the queue - a queue that looks stuck.
mtype must be strictly positive (mtype <= 0 is EINVAL), so a naive 'route 0 means default' encoding is rejected by the kernel.
MSG_EXCEPT and MSG_COPY are Linux/GNU extensions - routing that inverts or copies by type is not portable to other POSIX systems.
Queue ids and buffers are manual resources: without msgctl(IPC_RMID) and an explicit close path, abandoned queues and file descriptors survive the router.
